processing: Black tea from a working Nilgiri estate with its own factory, sited so that warm winds rising from the plains help the wither. The top grade comes from a clonal variety.
harvest_season: The peak quality season starts in January and can run to mid-March, with a second quality season in August and September.
appearance_dry: As with other orthodox Nilgiri blacks, dark twisted leaf; the finer grades are the ones to look at closely.
appearance_liquor: Typical of Nilgiri black tea, a clear, bright amber-copper.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown leaf, as is usual for Nilgiri black tea.
taste_profile: Little is documented about this garden's cup in particular. Nilgiri blacks in general are bright, brisk and lightly fruity rather than heavy.

brewing.notes: Western-style, as is usual for Nilgiri black tea. Pull it early if it starts to turn sharp.

vintage_note: Bought by season rather than by age: the January to March teas are the ones the garden itself regards as its best, with August and September as the second window. As with other Nilgiri blacks, drink it within a year or two of picking. Most of the crop goes abroad, so it reaches shops under an importer's lot name more often than as a branded estate tea.
description:
Havukal is a tea garden near Kotagiri in the Nilgiris of Tamil Nadu, one of the small group of southern estates noted for producing specialty lots alongside everyday tea. Its reputation rests on productivity and export more than on fame among home drinkers.

The factory was placed to catch warm air coming up from the plains, a natural help during withering. The best grade is made from a clonal variety and is sold at a premium.

Little is written about how this garden's tea tastes on its own terms. Expect what is typical of the Nilgiris: a bright, brisk cup with some fruit and flowers, better brewed for three or four minutes than stewed. It usually takes milk less gladly than a strong Assam does.

When buying, ask for the picking month. A January to March lot is the one to try first, and an August or September lot makes a fair comparison.
history: Little is documented about the garden's early years. The Thangavelu family bought Havukal in 1957 and has run it since, according to a trade press profile, which also credits it with an average of 4,031 kg of finished tea per hectare per year since 2009, among the highest in South India by some measures. About 85 percent of production is exported.
